steps.h: A question that opens a journey
steps.t: A question that opens a journey Mr Omar sells bread and bananas. Amal wants to understand how they got there. Press Next and hear the questions she constructs. Mr Omar sells bread and bananas. Amal wants to understand how they got there. Press Next and hear the questions she constructs. A good question about a topic is one you cannot answer yet, and it opens up a part of the topic you had not thought about. Food has a journey. Each question opens one stage of it. Where was the wheat in this bread grown? That opens the start of the journey. How many days did the banana travel? That opens the middle. Is bread nice? Everybody has an answer. It opens nothing. Children ask about themselves: do I like bananas? Ask about the topic: where did the banana come from, and how? Press Next and follow Amal's questions.

steps.h: The stages of a food journey
steps.t: The stages of a food journey Food travels in stages. Tap each stage; each one is a place a question can open. Food travels in stages. Tap each stage; each one is a place a question can open. Grown, moved, sold, eaten. Four stages. A question about each stage opens a different part of the topic. Tap all four, then answer.

Construct your questions about food You want to understand a stage of the food journey. Construct the question that opens it, then press Ask it . You want to understand a stage of the food journey. Construct the question that opens it, then press Ask it . Pick the question word that asks for the thing you want to understand, and the ending that names the stage. You want to understand where the wheat was grown. Where, plus was the wheat in our bread grown? Read the card, pick the word and the ending, press Ask it.

Does it open the journey? Our topic is the journey of our food. Would this question help you UNDERSTAND it? Our topic is the journey of our food. Would this question help you UNDERSTAND it? A question helps when you cannot answer it yet and it opens a stage of the journey. How far does a banana travel? Opens the moving stage. Helps. Are bananas yellow? Look at one. Does not help. What is my favourite fruit? About you, not the journey. Read it, then tap the bin.

steps.h: Locate the answers in the text

Read the question, then locate the sentence that answers it and nothing else. How many days does the journey take? Locate the sentence with the number of days. Why are they kept cold? Locate the sentence with the reason. Children tap the first sentence about bananas. Every sentence is about bananas. Locate the one that answers THIS question. Press Read it to me, then tap the sentence that answers.

Locate it in the market The market is a source about food journeys too. Explore it, then locate the part that answers each question. The market is a source about food journeys too. Explore it, then locate the part that answers each question. A picture holds answers as well as a text. Look for the PART of the picture that answers your question. Tap five things, then locate the part for each question.

Choose the way that fits Observe, ask, measure: you know all three. This year you CHOOSE the one that fits each question. Press Next . Observe, ask, measure: you know all three. This year you CHOOSE the one that fits each question. Press Next . An investigation picks the way that fits the question. What is on the ground: observe. What people do at home: ask. How much rain fell: measure. How many plastic cups are on the playground? You can see them: observe and count. What do you do with your carton at home? You cannot see that: ask. How much rain fell last night? A gauge measures it in millimetres. Children ask people about things they could count themselves. If you can see it, count it. Ask only what you cannot see. Press Next and match each question to its way.

Observe the playground after lunch Here is everything on the playground after lunch. Count one kind at a time: tap each one. Leaves are not litter, so leave them. Here is everything on the playground after lunch. Count one kind at a time: tap each one. Leaves are not litter, so leave them. Observing means counting what is really there, one kind at a time. Decide what counts before you start: leaves fell from the tree, so they are not litter. Count the plastic cups: tap every plastic cup. Five. Then the apple cores. Then the paper. Then the cartons. Children count everything they see, leaves included. Count only what you are looking for. Tap every plastic cup, then every apple core, then every piece of paper, then every carton.

What the litter count shows Your litter count as a bar chart. Look, then tap. Your litter count as a bar chart. Look, then tap. What you counted is now a chart. The longest bar is the litter there was most of. Read the question, look at the bars, tap.

A questionnaire asks everyone the same question with the same choices, so the answers can be counted. Ask, listen, record, six times.

The questionnaire as a table The carton answers as a table of numbers. Look, then tap. The carton answers as a table of numbers. Look, then tap. A table records findings as numbers. Read the number for each row, and add them for the total. Read the question, find the number, tap.

steps.h: Measure the rain for the compost
steps.t: Measure the rain for the compost The compost heap needs water. Every morning the class read the rain gauge, in millimetres. Read the measurements, then tap. The compost heap needs water. Every morning the class read the rain gauge, in millimetres. Read the measurements, then tap. A rain gauge measures how much rain fell, in millimetres. The longer the bar, the more rain that day. Tuesday: 12 millimetres. Monday: 4. How much more on Tuesday? 12 take away 4: 8 millimetres. Children say 'Tuesday was wetter' and stop. Measuring lets you say HOW MUCH wetter. Read the measurements, then tap.

steps.h: Which bin does it belong in?
steps.t: Which bin does it belong in? Everything we found can be recorded by where it should GO. Record each thing under recycling, compost, or rubbish. Everything we found can be recorded by where it should GO. Record each thing under recycling, compost, or rubbish. Recording findings means organising them into groups that make sense. For waste, the groups are where it should go. A tin can: recycling. An apple core: compost. It rots into soil. A sweet wrapper: rubbish. It cannot be recycled or composted. Read the thing, tap the group.

steps.h: A conclusion goes exactly as far as the data
steps.t: A conclusion goes exactly as far as the data A conclusion is a sentence the data proves. This year: it goes exactly as far as the data, and no further. Press Next . A conclusion is a sentence the data proves. This year: it goes exactly as far as the data, and no further. Press Next . The data proves what it proves. A conclusion that goes further than the data is a guess wearing a conclusion's clothes. Three of six slept eight to ten hours. Conclusion: half of the children we asked slept eight to ten hours. Children everywhere sleep eight to ten hours? We asked six children in one class. Too far. Children stretch a conclusion to the whole world. Say what THIS data proves about THESE people. Press Next and see how far a conclusion can go.

steps.h: Survey: how many hours did you sleep?
steps.t: Survey: how many hours did you sleep? Ask each classmate and record the answer. This is the data our conclusions will come from. Ask each classmate and record the answer. This is the data our conclusions will come from. First the data. Then the conclusions. Ask, listen, record, six times.

Draw conclusions from the bars Here is the sleep data as bars. Each question asks for a conclusion the bars PROVE. Look, then tap. Here is the sleep data as bars. Each question asks for a conclusion the bars PROVE. Look, then tap. A conclusion compares, adds up, or counts. More than, how many altogether, how many more. Eight to ten: 3. Less than eight: 2. More slept eight to ten than less than eight: yes. 2 + 3 + 1: six children altogether. Children answer from what they think happens. Every answer is in the bars. Read the question, look at the bars, tap.

steps.h: Conclusions from a table of numbers
steps.t: Conclusions from a table of numbers The class library counted the books borrowed each day for evening reading. Draw conclusions from the numbers. The class library counted the books borrowed each day for evening reading. Draw conclusions from the numbers. Numbers in a table can be compared, added and taken away, just like bars. Read the question, find the numbers, tap.

Proved, or too far? Our sleep chart says: less than 8 hours, 2; 8 to 10, 3; more than 10, 1. Does the data PROVE this sentence, or does it go too far? Our sleep chart says: less than 8 hours, 2; 8 to 10, 3; more than 10, 1. Does the data PROVE this sentence, or does it go too far? A conclusion is proved by the data and goes no further. A sentence about people we did not ask, or things we did not measure, goes too far. Half of the children we asked slept 8 to 10 hours: proved. Three of six. Sami is always tired: we asked about ONE night. Too far. Read the sentence, then tap the bin.

Indoors, outdoors, or both? A diagram with two circles that overlap. Some evening activities happen indoors, some outdoors, some both. Record each one in the right part. A diagram with two circles that overlap. Some evening activities happen indoors, some outdoors, some both. Record each one in the right part. A Venn diagram has two circles that overlap. Only in the left, only in the right, or in the middle where both are true. Watching television: indoors. Football: outdoors. Reading a comic: you can do it either way. The middle. Children put everything in the middle. The middle is only for things that are really BOTH. Read the activity, tap the part of the diagram.

Conclusions and diagrams Think about conclusions and the Venn diagram. Tap the answer. Think about conclusions and the Venn diagram. Tap the answer. A conclusion goes as far as the data and no further. A Venn diagram shows one group, the other, or both. Read it, then tap.

One field, four views Everybody knows the same facts about the old field. They still think different things. Press Next . Everybody knows the same facts about the old field. They still think different things. Press Next . People can know the same facts and think different things, because each person is affected differently. A shopkeeper, a parent, a farmer and a company look at the same field from four places. Mr Omar thinks the supermarket will close his shop. Mrs Farah thinks it will make food cheaper for her four children. Same field, opposite views, and both have reasons. Children decide one person is right and the rest are wrong. Ask what each person stands to gain or lose. That is where views come from. Press Next and hear four views.

Who thinks what? Teacher Yasmin describes a view. Who holds it? Tap the person. Teacher Yasmin describes a view. Who holds it? Tap the person. Recognising that people think different things means being able to say WHO thinks WHAT, and why they might. The supermarket will close small shops: that is the shopkeeper. Eighty jobs: that is the supermarket company. Read the view, then tap the person who holds it.

steps.h: A fact, or what somebody thinks?
steps.t: A fact, or what somebody thinks? Some of these are facts about the old field. Some are what a person THINKS should happen. Which is it? Some of these are facts about the old field. Some are what a person THINKS should happen. Which is it? A fact is true for everybody. A view is what one person thinks should happen. Other people can think differently. The field is at the edge of town: a fact. The supermarket should be built: what Dana thinks. Read it, then tap the bin.

The company's leaflet The supermarket company handed out a leaflet at the market. Find the sentences that show what the AUTHOR thinks. Then say what the viewpoint is. The supermarket company handed out a leaflet at the market. Find the sentences that show what the AUTHOR thinks. Then say what the viewpoint is. A source is written by somebody, and that somebody has a viewpoint. Look for the sentences that show what the author wants to happen, and the reasons they give. Eighty new jobs for local people: that is the author's reason. We hope you will support the plan: that is what the author wants. Children take a leaflet as plain facts. Ask: who wrote this, and what do THEY want from me? Press Read it to me, then tap the sentences.

The shopkeeper's letter Mr Omar wrote a letter to the town newspaper. Find HIS viewpoint. Is it the same as the leaflet's? Mr Omar wrote a letter to the town newspaper. Find HIS viewpoint. Is it the same as the leaflet's? A different author, a different viewpoint. Both are about the same field. Read it, then tap the sentences.

steps.h: What do YOU think of their views?
steps.t: What do YOU think of their views? Now you. Do you agree with Mr Omar? With Mrs Farah? With Mr Hassan? Say what you think of each view, with two reasons. Now you. Do you agree with Mr Omar? With Mrs Farah? With Mr Hassan? Say what you think of each view, with two reasons. An opinion about somebody else's viewpoint says whether you agree, and why. Two reasons, both about the topic. I partly agree with Mr Omar, because small shops do close when big ones open, and because he knows his customers. Because I like chips is not a reason about the old field. Children just say 'I agree' and stop. Say why. Twice. Tap what you think, then two reasons.

Views and viewpoints Think about who thinks what, the leaflet, the letter and your opinions. Tap the answer. Think about who thinks what, the leaflet, the letter and your opinions. Tap the answer. People think different things. An author has a viewpoint. You can have an opinion about it, with reasons. Read it, then tap.
